turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late, the tram just sat there at Flinders for ages and then the car park was packed. We left the flat at half nine thinking we'd be early, so yeah, bit embarrassing.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, no stress. Grab a seat, both of you.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm his partner, Sam. We got turned around near the lifts as well, the signs are a bit hopeless.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Happens all the time. So what can I do for you today?

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, well, it's kind of two things tangled up. My older sister got told a few months back she's got a thyroid problem, overactive they reckon, and Sam's been on at me to get checked ever since. But the thing that's actually worrying me, the reason I booked, is I've been dropping weight even though I'm eating more than usual, and my heart keeps racing.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. We'll come back to your sister in a minute. Tell me a bit more about the weight and the heart.

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): So the weight, um, my jeans are all loose and I've gone in two notches on the belt, and I used to sit around eighty two kilos easy. I'm eating heaps though, bigger breakfast than I used to, second breakfast sometimes, and I'm still hungry by the time I get home. And the heart thing, it'll just take off, like thumping fast, even if I'm standing at the bench not doing much.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he's been sweating. Like the sheets are damp some nights, and his hands go shaky when he's trying to do something fiddly.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah that's fair, the sweating is pretty much every day now, not just nights, and the shaky hands, um, when I'm plating up or even holding a coffee the cup rattles. It's not all the time but most days.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long's all this been going on for?

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): That's the annoying bit, err, I can't actually date it. It was last winter, or maybe the winter before, around when we shifted flats or after that, I lose track. Not like a sudden week, more a slow creep, but I couldn't tell you the month.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with the racing heart?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no chest pain. I kept waiting for it, you know, because you read stuff, but it's just the fast thump, no pain, no tightness.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): And no fevers? Short of breath at all?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever. Breath's ok too, I can still get up the stairs at the flat, I just feel revved up while I'm doing it.

[SEG0016] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry to jump in, obs are done. Pulse is a hundred and twelve, blood pressure's one thirty two over seventy eight, temp's thirty six point six, oxygen sats ninety eight percent, and weight today is seventy six kilograms.

[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. So, dropping weight from about eighty two down to seventy six, eating more, heart racing, sweating most days, shaky hands, and you can't pin when it started. No chest pain, no fever, breathing's ok. Pulse is up at a hundred and twelve.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah that sounds right. Umm, eighty two was sort of my steady weight for years, like all through my twenties, I'm twenty nine now.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines? And have you tried any of your sister's tablets?

[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't touched her stuff, she offered and I said no. I do take a tablet of esomaprazole by mouth, twenty milligram, every morning for the reflux, have done since uni pretty much. And I was on vitamin D, a thousand units, but I stopped that about a month ago because I kept forgetting the bottle.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing. No drug allergies, no food ones, I can eat whatever at the cafe.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): And family, apart from your older sister's thyroid. Anyone else with thyroid, diabetes, heart problems?

[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, let me do the whole lot so I don't miss someone. My father had diabetes in his fifties, type two, he's still on tablets for it, and my mother did not, she's never had sugar problems. My other sister, the younger one, has pressure but no sugar, they checked her and it was fine. No heart attacks that I know of, that's everyone, just the three of us kids.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you do for work, and how's the rest of life, food, exercise, drink?

[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Ok so work, I'm a chef at a little cafe in Fitzroy, been there four years, and the hours are early, I start at six most mornings and I'm usually done around three, though if we've got a function I stay till nine for the dinner service maybe two nights a week. Diet wise I eat a lot of what we cook, big breakfast on the line, then I pick through the day, toasties, cake, whatever's left, and I still have dinner at home. Exercise, I used to ride my bike in but it's been in the shed for months, now I just walk the dog a few times a week, like three times, not far. Alcohol, I don't drink through the week, Friday I'll have three or four beers and maybe a couple on Saturday, that's about it.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The dog walks are real, I can vouch for that. And he really doesn't drink in the week, I've never seen him.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me play that back. Chef, early starts from six, sometimes through to nine, eating a lot of the cafe food plus dinner, bike's been put away, dog walks a few times a week, a few beers Friday and Saturday. Dad with diabetes, younger sister with blood pressure but not diabetes, mum clear of it, older sister with the overactive thyroid. And you haven't taken her medication.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Yep. That's the lot. I overthink it, sorry.

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you hold your hands out flat for me. Mm, there's a fine shake there, and your palms are a bit sweaty, and the pulse is fast but regular. I'll just feel your neck. Thyroid doesn't feel enlarged.

[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah the shake shows up when I'm trying to tweeze microgreens onto a plate, which is ridiculous, it takes me twice as long. And the sweat's worse over the grill, uh, I drip into the pass sometimes.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, I think this may be an overactive thyroid, the weight coming off while you're eating more, the fast heart, the sweat and the shake, plus your sister's history. That's a working impression, not a diagnosis, the bloods have to confirm it. Anxiety can speed the heart up too, but it doesn't usually make you lose weight while you're eating more, so thyroid is what I'm chasing first.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange thyroid blood tests and a general blood screen, and an ECG given that pulse. All of that can be done today, the nurse will sort the ECG at the desk and I'll give you a path form for the bloods.
[SEG0034] person_4 (NURSE): I can book the ECG for straight after this, there's a slot. Bloods, you'll take the form down to pathology, they're open till four.

[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): So if it is the thyroid, is that the same as my sister, because she was talking about carbimazole and I, uh, got halfway through the leaflet and freaked myself out about side effects. That's why I wouldn't take any of hers.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't start anything today, and definitely don't take her carbimazole. If the tests show an overactive thyroid we can talk options then, it isn't always the same tablet. Side effects are a conversation for once we actually know.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): How soon do we come back?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book a review in a fortnight and we'll go through the results together. Reception can set that as you leave.

[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): And should I keep eating like this or pull back, because part of me thinks if I eat less the weight thing looks more normal, but I'm starving if I try. I did two days last week of just the breakfast and I was shaky and ratty by four.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Eat when you're hungry, don't try to starve it down, that won't help us and you'll feel worse. If the heart starts hurting, or you feel faint, or you can't catch your breath, go to emergency rather than waiting for the fortnight. Otherwise we'll see you with the results.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Ok. I'll try not to google the whole night. Thanks for actually listening to the long version, I know I go on.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): You gave me what I needed. See you in a fortnight.

spec.situation: Younger adult losing weight with a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaky hands, eats more than usual; hair thinning not mentioned; a sister has thyroid disease; blood tests and ECG planned.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

omissions.text: Patient denied both chest pain and chest tightness with the racing heart.
Vitamin D 1000 units was stopped about a month ago because the patient kept forgetting it.
Mother has never had diabetes/'sugar problems'.
No heart attacks known in the family.
Doctor noted anxiety as an alternative explanation for the fast heart, but said it would not usually cause weight loss despite increased eating, so thyroid was being pursued first.
Nurse stated ECG could be booked straight after the consultation and pathology was open until 4 pm.

Shaky hands affect function, e.g. cup rattles when holding coffee and difficulty plating/tweezing microgreens, taking twice as long.
Patient denied taking sister's medication before today: he has not touched her tablets despite her offering them.
